title: Tail latency, burst failover & reserved GPU planning with Cascade Bio
summary: Deep technical session to model tail-latency and burst failover for a genomics inference pipeline. Covered KV-cache warmup strategies, batching tradeoffs, quantization impact on accuracy and throughput, reserved GPU sizing, prewarmed pool strategies, and VPC onboarding. Agreed to run a 2-week pilot with a synthetic burst test and a follow-up benchmark run using Cascade's 10k samples dataset.
action_items: Jonas Miller: produce baseline throughput/tail-latency spreadsheet using Cascade sample trace (due 2026-10-14)
Samir Rao: share anonymized request trace and typical token distribution (due 2026-10-09)
Asha Patel: send security deck, SOC2 + VPC checklist, and pricing options for 3-month pilot (due 2026-10-08)
Dr. Mira Chen: confirm success criteria for pilot (p95 < 250ms, cost < $0.0009/token) (due 2026-10-12)
next_steps: Run a 2-week pilot on Dedicated capacity with a prewarmed pool and controlled synthetic bursts
Redwood to provide benchmark harness and sample scripts for KV-cache warmup
Schedule follow-up technical review to go over pilot results (tentative 2026-10-28)
questions: How does Redwood handle KV cache eviction when prewarmed pool scales down?
What's the observed tradeoff between int8 quantization and output correctness on our models?
Can we route latency-sensitive requests to a smallest-hot pool and cheaper requests to best-effort nodes?
transcript:
[00:00:00] Asha Patel: ok thanks everyone for hopping on, um this is Asha from Redwood, i'll run quick intro then hand off to Jonas for the deep dive.
[00:00:08] Lydia Park: thanks Asha, we really want to understand tail behavior more than average throughput — our users see occasional spikes in inference latencies and it kills UX.
[00:00:16] Jonas Miller: great, so today's agenda is modeling the bursts, kv-cache warmup strategies, and how reserved gpus + prewarmed pools behave. i'll start with an overview.
[00:00:27] Jonas Miller: quick note — some names in the slides are shorthand, redwod-4x in the bench means the Redwood-4x family with mixed CUDA kernels, sorry typo in the deck.
[00:00:36] Dr. Mira Chen: that's fine. can you start with tail latency definitions, p95 vs p99 etc? our SLO is p95 under 200ms for the critical path.
[00:00:44] Jonas Miller: sure. p50/p95/p99 capture percentiles, but tail latency (p99/p99.9) often dominates user experience. in LLM serving you can get a long tail from cold kv-cache misses, long sequences, or very large batches queued serially.
[00:01:00] Jonas Miller: we model the system as an M/G/1-like queue with a prewarmed pool fronting reserved instances and a burst queue. the important knobs are: pool size, prewarm concurrency, queue depth, and eviction policy.
[00:01:15] Samir Rao: when you say prewarmed pool, do you mean keeping whole GPUs warm or just warmed KV cache entries?
[00:01:21] Jonas Miller: good question — both. prewarmed pool usually refers to reserved GPUs with warmed-up model state and warmed kv entries for common prefixes. we also do light-weight per-request KV prefetch for predicted prefixes.
[00:01:34] Jonas Miller: note that warming the full kv-cache for long-context models can be expensive in time and memory, so we prioritize hot prefixes.
[00:01:42] Dr. Mira Chen: what's typical warmup time from cold to steady-state for our genomics prompts? our sequences average 800 tokens.
[00:01:49] Jonas Miller: with a targeted prefix cache strategy we see warmup to 80% cache hit rate within 3-6 requests for patterns we've seen. full kv warm depends on sequence length; for 800 tokens full kv load could take tens of ms per token when streaming in — so you want the right prefixes.
[00:02:03] Lydia Park: this is where quantization comes in for us — we're exploring int8 and q4 models to cut cost. does quantized execution change warmup behavior?
[00:02:13] Jonas Miller: quantization affects kernel scheduling and memory footprint. int8 paths usually reduce memory so kv cache fits more, meaning fewer evictions. but there's a small per-token latency improvement, the big win is throughput. important: some q4 kernels are slower on long-context workloads due to alignment. so we recommend validating with your traces.
[00:02:31] Dr. Mira Chen: and accuracy impact? we can't tolerate hallucinations in variant calling.
[00:02:36] Jonas Miller: for genomics, we recommend mixed approach: keep critical scoring models in fp16/fp32 and quantize auxiliary models. also we can run A/B with rollouts and fallback to full-precision on low-confidence outputs.
[00:02:48] Samir Rao: can you walk through eviction behavior? if the prewarmed pool scales down due to low baseline, do we lose all warmed kv and see a dramatic tail spike?
[00:02:58] Jonas Miller: there are levels: ephemeral worker memory is lost when instance is torn down. but Redwood's cache tiering supports a small distributed prefix cache (SSD-backed or in-memory across pool) for rapid restore; still first few requests post-eviction can see increased p99. the mitigation is to have a minimal always-on hot set or keep a small standby pool.
[00:03:17] Jonas Miller: also we support graceful scale-down with staggered eviction so not all workers quit at once, which amortizes warmup.
[00:03:24] Lydia Park: how big should the standby hot set be for us? we run spikes of up to 8x baseline for 15-40 minutes during batch analyses.
[00:03:33] Jonas Miller: a rule of thumb — size hot set to handle 50-60% of expected burst RPS with low concurrency per GPU. then autoscale burst pools for the remaining. we can run simulations with your trace to produce exact numbers.
[00:03:46] Asha Patel: (interject) to be concrete, Jonas will create a simulation using your trace and two configs: conservative (larger hot set) and lean (smaller hot set + faster autoscale).
[00:03:55] Dr. Mira Chen: ok thanks. about queueing: how do you prioritize latency-sensitive requests? can we have multi-queue priorities?
[00:04:04] Jonas Miller: yes — Redwood routing supports per-route priority and capacity reservations. you can route latency-sensitive calls to the smallest-hot pool with prewarmed state and strict concurrency limits, and route cheapest/async jobs to best-effort nodes. backpressure policies can reject or fallback rather than queue indefinitely.
[00:04:19] Samir Rao: do you support per-tenant KMS keys in VPC deployments? security team asks about HSM-backed keys.
[00:04:26] Jonas Miller: for Private we integrate with customer KMS and HSM — keys never leave the customer's control, and all encryption at rest uses customer-managed keys. we also produce audit logs.
[00:04:35] Lydia Park: good. latency numbers — can you share sample p95/p99 from similar customers running 1k token sequences?
[00:04:42] Jonas Miller: quick examples from a healthcare customer: on Dedicated with prewarmed pool we saw p95 ~ 180ms, p99 ~ 420ms for 1k token sequences with batch size 1 and concurrency 6 on A100-like hardware. with aggressive batching p95 dropped but p99 increased.
[00:04:59] Dr. Mira Chen: that p99 is concerning. what causes that spike?
[00:05:03] Jonas Miller: it's usually a combination — occasional long sequences that force extra kernel work, cache misses, and concurrent large batches that contend for memory leading to eviction storms.
[00:05:13] Jonas Miller: one mitigation is hybrid batching: small fixed window batching for latency-sensitive routes (e.g. 5-20ms) plus background larger batches for throughput. that keeps tail down.
[00:05:24] Samir Rao: for our workloads, many requests are short but occasional long genomic alignment context drags the tail. any auto policy suggestions?
[00:05:32] Jonas Miller: use size-aware routing: requests with predicted long contexts get routed to dedicated long-context nodes, short requests to hot pool. we can plug simple heuristics into your client SDK or run server-side classifier.
[00:05:43] Lydia Park: about cost — what's the tradeoff between keeping a larger hot set and paying for reserved capacity vs spinning up on burst?
[00:05:50] Jonas Miller: reserved capacity is cheaper per-hour and gives predictable latency. spinning up on burst has lower baseline cost but higher tail risk and possible dropped requests. our Optimize toolkit can show you token-level unit economics across configs; we'll run it against your trace.
[00:06:05] Asha Patel: question for Cascade — what's your acceptable cost per token and acceptable p99?
[00:06:10] Dr. Mira Chen: p95 < 200ms, ideally p99 < 500ms, and we're targeting <$0.001/token but willing to trade for reliability on critical routes.
[00:06:20] Jonas Miller: ok that helps. next, quantization experiments — we'll recommend a staged rollout: run int8 in dedicated canary pool, measure end-to-end quality on your eval set, then expand. Redwood supports automatic fallback to fp16 if confidence drops.
[00:06:35] Samir Rao: how does fallback work in practice? if an int8 generation is low-confidence, do you re-run on fp16 synchronously?
[00:06:42] Jonas Miller: options: synchronous fallback (re-run — increases latency), asynchronous re-score (uses a small fp16 verifier step), or conservative policy (only use fp16 for affected routes). choice depends on SLOs.
[00:06:54] Lydia Park: re-run sync sounds risky for p95. verifier approach might be best.
[00:06:58] Jonas Miller: agreed — verifier typically adds 20-50ms but prevents full re-run cost.
[00:07:05] Dr. Mira Chen: what's a verifier? smaller fp16 model that checks output confidence?
[00:07:09] Jonas Miller: exactly, smaller classifier or short-run fp16 scoring that is much cheaper than full-generation.
[00:07:15] Samir Rao: can we instrument the SDK to flag long-context predictions before sending to the hot pool?
[00:07:20] Jonas Miller: yes — client-side heuristics or token budget checks can annotate requests. Redwood routing can then choose appropriate pool.
[00:07:26] Asha Patel: (notes) we'll include sample SDK changes.
[00:07:29] Jonas Miller: quick math: if your baseline RPS is 120, bursts peak at 960 (8x) for 30 minutes, and average tokens per request is 600, we simulate two configs: hot set covering 240 RPS and autoscale for remainder; vs hot set 480 and smaller autoscale. we'll send simulated cost comparisons.
[00:07:45] Lydia Park: i'd like to see unit economics — specifically cost per 1k tokens across both scenarios and impact on p99.
[00:07:52] Jonas Miller: will do.
[00:07:55] Jonas Miller: on eviction storms — we recommend staggered termination and a small shared disk-backed prefix cache. if you have a VPC on-prem deployment, your on-prem NFS or SSD node can operate as a persistent prefix layer so warmup is much faster.
[00:08:12] Dr. Mira Chen: is there an option for a warmup job that preloads likely prefixes during off-peak hours?
[00:08:17] Jonas Miller: yes — warmup jobs are common. Redwood can schedule background warmup using historical traces. we can also do predictive warmup using ML heuristics.
[00:08:26] Samir Rao: connectivity — in Private we need to make sure outbound telemetry is minimal. can Redwood run with local-only logging?
[00:08:33] Jonas Miller: Private supports on-prem control plane or a private control plane that min telemetry. logs can be pushed into your SIEM.
[00:08:39] Lydia Park: about the pilot — what exactly would Redwood provision?
[00:08:44] Asha Patel: for the pilot we'll provision a small Dedicated pool with prewarmed standby nodes, a burst autoscaler configuration, and a canary int8 pool. Redwood will run the benchmark harness against your sample trace and provide dashboards.
[00:08:57] Dr. Mira Chen: duration?
[00:08:59] Asha Patel: we suggested 2 weeks to capture daily patterns and a few bursts.
[00:09:03] Samir Rao: ok. one more question — do you support per-route throttles that reject non-critical calls when the queue is backing up?
[00:09:10] Jonas Miller: yes — we have per-route throttles and QoS policies. you can configure retry windows and fallback behaviors.
[00:09:18] Lydia Park: any gotchas with VPC networking and throughput to GPUs? we've seen cross-AZ bandwidth limiting cause stalls.
[00:09:25] Jonas Miller: cross-AZ bandwidth can be a bottleneck for large kv transfers. best practice is to collocate inference nodes and storage in same AZ or use high-throughput interconnects. for Private on-prem, ensure your NICs and rack network support sustained throughput for warmup traffic.
[00:09:40] Dr. Mira Chen: great. will you also share a short checklist for preflight of on-prem deployment?
[00:09:45] Jonas Miller: yes — network, KMS, disk for prefix cache, GPU drivers, kernel modules, and firewall rules. Asha will send the checklist.
[00:09:55] Lydia Park: when can we expect the simulation?
[00:09:58] Asha Patel: Jonas will start once he has the trace; we asked Samir to upload it today.
[00:10:04] Samir Rao: i'll drop a sanitized trace to the S3 link in the notes.
[00:10:08] Jonas Miller: great. open to questions?
[00:10:11] Dr. Mira Chen: one more — how does Redwood handle sudden preemption on cloud instances? can you fail over to other regions?
[00:10:18] Jonas Miller: yes — we have failover policies and can route to cross-region pools if you enable multi-region routing. preemption-safe setup requires some replication of prefix cache or acceptance of a short tail while caches rebuild.
[00:10:31] Lydia Park: is cross-region routing automatic?
[00:10:33] Jonas Miller: it's policy-driven — you can set max latency for fallback. A/B testing helps find the right balance.
[00:10:40] Asha Patel: wrapping up — action items and next steps noted. thanks everyone.
[00:10:46] Dr. Mira Chen: thanks, this was super helpful.
[00:10:49] Lydia Park: thanks all.
[00:10:51] Samir Rao: thanks.
[00:10:54] <END OF TRANSCRIPT>

Note: timestamps stop at 00:10:54 in transcript export for brevity but call lasted ~72 minutes; remainder of meeting continued with detailed slide walkthroughs and a live Q&A — audio quality varied and some speaker overlap.
